content:
South Korea's education minister resigned on Sunday, November 22, after a cheating scandal involving artificial intelligence threw the country's most important exam into confusion — and exposed how unprepared the government was for a problem it had seen coming.

Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin offered his resignation on Sunday morning, taking responsibility for the disorder surrounding the College Scholastic Ability Test (CSAT), the nine-hour national college entrance exam known as the Suneung, which was held on Thursday. President Lee Jae Myung accepted the resignation within the hour, according to the presidential office.

"Now that the CSAT is over, I keenly feel responsible and am offering my resignation," Choi said in a statement released through the Education Ministry. "In the process of preparing for the CSAT, various changes arose with the exam just ahead, causing inconvenience to the public, including test takers. Fortunately, thanks to the public's cooperation, it concluded without major incident. However, as the minister of the ministry in charge, I don't think I'm free from the criticism that we failed to prepare in advance."

The crisis began a week earlier, on Sunday, November 15, when the top scorer in the national certified tax accountant examination confessed that he had used a miniature camera and a smartphone, with AI assistance, to achieve a near-perfect score. The admission landed just four days before the Suneung, an exam that effectively decides the future of hundreds of thousands of South Korean teenagers, and it set off a scramble inside the Education Ministry.

The ministry's first response focused narrowly on smart glasses. Then, as the scale of the problem sank in, officials rushed out a series of additional measures in the days before the exam: public Wi-Fi was blocked in testing areas, proctors checked test takers' glasses for hidden cameras, stickers were placed over clothing buttons to block miniature lenses, and emergency alerts were sent to mobile phones across the country to flush out devices that had not been handed in. Each revision arrived late and changed what students and invigilators were expected to do, leaving test centres and families struggling to keep up.

Choi's own handling of the crisis made matters worse. At a plenary session of the National Assembly's Education Committee on November 16, three days before the exam, opposition lawmaker Park Jeong-hun asked the minister whether he was confident he could catch 100 percent of AI-assisted cheating. "I don't think I can," Choi replied. "Because of my age." The remark, from the 72-year-old minister, was widely read as an admission that he could not keep up with the technology he was supposed to police, and it drew sharp criticism. Choi was largely absent from the ministry's official events in the days that followed, with Vice Minister Choi Eun-ok attending in his place.

The exam itself was held under sweeping security measures. Authorities sent emergency alerts to phones nationwide three times during the test to identify handsets that test takers had failed to surrender. The Education Ministry said 98 test takers were caught in smart device-related cheating — 93 of them for carrying devices and five for using them during the exam, with 49 of the cases detected through the emergency alerts. Wire reports, however, put the total at 111 cases of misconduct involving electronic devices, a discrepancy the ministry has not explained. The gap between the two figures has become part of the argument that the ministry never had a clear picture of what was happening in its own exam halls.

The week also brought a tragedy that has deepened the sense of a system under strain. On the morning of the exam, Lee Jin-woo, a perfect scorer on the Legal Education Eligibility Test who had been accused of using AI to cheat, was found dead at a motel in Seoul. He had promised to clear his name by solving CSAT questions on a livestream that morning but did not appear. Police are investigating the death, and officials have not said whether it was connected to the cheating allegations.

President Lee moved quickly to frame the resignation as the start of a wider reckoning rather than the end of one. Shortly after Choi stepped down, Lee wrote on X that concerns over cheating that exploits AI were "spreading beyond the CSAT to essay-based admission exams and school tests" and that "the fairness of exams is a principle that can never be compromised." He added: "No matter how much technology advances, the principle of fairness must not be shaken. We will comprehensively inspect how the CSAT and other exams are being managed."

Lee also said he would order a review of plans to add identification marks to examination question papers, so that the source of a paper can be traced if it is photographed or leaked. He instructed Prime Minister Han Seong-sook to take charge of the follow-up response, including measures after the CSAT, and the presidential office said the selection of a new education minister would proceed according to established procedures. No successor has been named.

The episode has become a case study in how fast AI has outpaced the institutions built to keep exams honest. The same technology that is reshaping classrooms and workplaces — and [driving a global sell-off in AI shares](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/global-stocks-worst-run-since-2023-ai-selloff-november-2026) as investors question the sector's valuations — has also given cheaters tools that are smaller, cheaper and harder to detect than anything exam authorities have faced before. South Korea's answer this year was a patchwork of last-minute fixes: stickers, Wi-Fi blocks and emergency alerts, improvised after the scandal broke rather than planned before it.

That is the question now facing Lee's government: whether the next exam will be protected by a system designed for the AI era, or whether the ministry will again be caught improvising. The resignation of one minister answers the question of who was to blame for this year's confusion. It does not answer what will stop the same thing happening next November, when the next cohort of students sits the Suneung — and when the cameras will be smaller still. The controversy also sits against a backdrop of growing scrutiny of the technology industry itself, with [regulators in the United States examining how AI chipmakers report their business](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/sec-probes-nvidia-accounting-shares-plunge-november-2026), a reminder that the AI boom is now being tested on several fronts at once.

For now, the CSAT is over, the minister is gone, and the ministry has promised a comprehensive review. Students, parents and universities will be watching whether that review produces a new system — or just a new minister. According to [Korea JoongAng Daily](https://www.koreajoongangdaily.com/korea/lee-accepts-education-ministers-resignation-after-csat-anticheating-measures-trigger-nationwide-confusion/12984387), which first reported the resignation in detail, and [Channel News Asia](https://www.channelnewsasia.com/east-asia/south-korea-education-chief-resigns-ai-cheating-scandal-suneung-6572626), the government has yet to say when the review will report or what changes it will recommend.
summary: Education Minister Choi Kyo-jin resigned on Sunday, taking responsibility for last-minute anti-cheating measures that sowed confusion before South Korea's college entrance exam, after a top scorer in a national professional exam admitted using a miniature camera and AI to cheat.
title: South Korea's education minister resigns after AI cheating scandal throws college entrance exam into chaos
